identity.title: When does a funnel become a trap? A Gomboc-inspired model of protein folding landscapes.

content.abstract: The protein folding problem remains a fundamental challenge in biophysics. While energy landscape theory resolves Levinthal's paradox through funnel-shaped landscapes, the quantitative effects of landscape ruggedness on folding kinetics are not fully understood. We introduce a computational model inspired by Gomboc, a convex 3D shape with one stable equilibrium and one unstable equilibrium, as an analogy for protein folding landscapes. Using a tunable ruggedness parameter, we simulate "folding" across multiple ruggedness conditions (r = 0 and r = 10(-8) to 10(-3)), spanning five orders of magnitude in the positive-r regime. At minimal ruggedness (10(-8)), the model achieves 83% success in reaching native-like states. Increasing the ruggedness to 10(-7)-10(-5) reduces the success rate to 25-39%, reflecting landscape trapping as an analog for kinetic trapping in physical folding. Benchmarking against the TPR1 domain via Rosetta and AlphaFold3 reveals native-like coverages of 77% and 90%, respectively, showing qualitative correspondence with the Gomboc model's success rates at low ruggedness. These findings suggest that the Gomboc-inspired model captures essential features of folding landscape quality and may serve as a useful heuristic for comparing foldability across different systems, bridging mathematical topology with protein biophysics.
